title: The kill switch for harmful genes - Works in Progress Magazine
gist: siRNA gene-silencing drugs have solved the delivery problem for the liver (via GalNAc-sugar-tagged 'naked' siRNA), turning gene silencing into a programmable, sequence-swappable medicine platform; the next multi-year race is extending that delivery breakthrough to the brain (Alzheimer's), kidneys, lungs, fat, and muscle, with Alnylam and Arrowhead as the lead competitors.

themes.theme: Why small-molecule drug discovery is structurally limited

insights.claim: The majority of human proteins are 'undruggable' because current small-molecule chemistry cannot bind them, either because they lack a physical pocket for a drug to attach to or because they are intrinsically disordered with no stable structure.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: This structural ceiling on small-molecule chemistry is the core reason RNA-based and gene-editing platforms (siRNA, ASOs, CRISPR) have an addressable-market advantage over traditional pharma R&D for a large share of disease targets.
insights.quote: The majority of human proteins are considered ‘undruggable’, meaning that none of the small molecules we can currently synthesize can effectively bind to them
insights.locator: It’s worse than this: medicinal chemists struggle

insights.claim: Drug discovery concentrates on the minority of druggable protein targets not because those targets are the most medically important, but because they are the only ones current chemistry can reach, a streetlight-effect bias in R&D allocation.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Investors should discount the apparent scarcity of new small-molecule targets as a chemistry limitation, not a biology limitation — implying platforms that bypass small-molecule chemistry unlock previously invisible target space.
insights.quote: Drug discovery ends up focusing on the minority of targets that are druggable, like the proverbial drunk searching for his keys under the streetlamp because that’s where the light shines.
insights.locator: The majority of human proteins are considered

insights.claim: Even for druggable targets, most drugs fail in clinical trials because a chemical designed to hit one protein cleanly and do nothing else almost never behaves that way in the body, being broken down early, hitting off-target proteins, or failing to reach the right tissue.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: This is the base-rate explanation for high clinical attrition in small-molecule pharma pipelines, a reason to favor platforms with more predictable mechanism-of-action behavior.
insights.locator: In practice, this almost never goes as planned

themes.theme: How siRNA was discovered and how it works

insights.claim: siRNA-based gene silencing was discovered by accident in 1990 when scientists at DNA Plant Technology Corporation tried to make petunias darker by adding an extra pigment-gene copy, and instead the flowers turned white, a phenomenon they called 'cosuppression'.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A reminder that major therapeutic platforms can originate from unrelated basic-science accidents, useful context for how far upstream today's biotech pipelines can trace their origin.
insights.locator: The story of siRNA begins in 1990

insights.claim: Andrew Fire and Craig Mello won a Nobel Prize for identifying siRNA as the mechanism behind cosuppression, establishing RNA interference as a real biological pathway that could later be engineered into medicine.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Marks the scientific origin point of a therapeutic category that took roughly two more decades to reach its first FDA approval, useful for timeline-of-innovation benchmarking in biotech.
insights.locator: Andrew Fire and Craig Mello later won a Nobel prize

insights.claim: siRNA works by binding to a specific messenger RNA sequence like a matching barcode and marking it for destruction by the cell's own gene-silencing machinery, which prevents the corresponding protein from ever being made.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: This sequence-specific mechanism is what makes siRNA reprogrammable across diseases simply by changing the target sequence, the core economic advantage of the platform.
insights.locator: That’s exactly what siRNA, or ‘small interfering RNA’, does

themes.theme: Solving the delivery problem: from lipid nanoparticles to naked siRNA

insights.claim: Naked siRNA injected directly into the bloodstream does nothing useful because it faces three sequential barriers: destruction by RNA-degrading enzymes in the blood, inability to cross the cell membrane on its own, and digestion inside the endosome after cell entry.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: This three-part delivery framework is the actual technical moat in RNA therapeutics — companies are effectively competing on solving this exact sequence of problems, not on discovering new gene targets.
insights.locator: If you just injected siRNA into a patient’s veins

insights.claim: Viral delivery vectors for siRNA face a structural ceiling because the immune system has evolved over hundreds of millions of years to detect and destroy viruses, making repeated dosing risky and reducing efficacy over time.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Explains why viral-vector siRNA delivery has largely been sidelined in favor of lipid nanoparticle and conjugate chemistry approaches for chronic, repeat-dose treatments.
insights.locator: But viruses come with a drawback

insights.claim: The breakthrough that made lipid nanoparticle delivery viable was 'ionizable lipids' that stay neutral in the bloodstream (minimizing tissue damage) but turn positively charged inside the acidic endosome, destabilizing it and releasing the siRNA into the cell.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: This chemistry insight, refined over more than a decade into a roughly thousand-fold potency improvement, is the platform technology underlying every currently marketed siRNA drug's delivery system.
insights.quote: These lipids are neutral in the bloodstream, minimizing damage, but turn positive once inside an endosome, as endosomes are acidic.
insights.locator: The next breakthrough was more subtle

insights.claim: Patisiran, approved by the FDA in 2018 as the first RNA interference drug, used ionizable lipid nanoparticles to silence the mutated transthyretin gene in liver cells and proved siRNA could work as an actual medicine, but its delivery method was already being surpassed by newer chemistry by the time it launched.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A landmark regulatory approval that also functioned as a technological dead-end for its own delivery method within a few years, illustrating how fast the RNA therapeutics platform is still moving.
insights.locator: Patisiran, the first FDA-approved siRNA drug

insights.claim: Alnylam Pharmaceuticals engineered chemically modified siRNA, replacing the reactive oxygen atom in RNA's backbone with fluorine, hydrogen, or a methyl group, to make the molecule stable enough to survive in the bloodstream without any protective carrier ('naked' siRNA).
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Eliminating the need for a lipid nanoparticle carrier simplifies manufacturing, reduces immune risk, and enabled the shift to far less frequent dosing schedules.
insights.locator: By chemically modifying that pesky oxygen

insights.claim: Naked siRNA is directed specifically to the liver by attaching three copies of the sugar molecule GalNAc, which liver cells' surface receptors recognize and pull inside via their endosomes, functioning as a molecular address label instead of a lipid carrier.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The GalNAc-conjugate approach is the current gold-standard delivery chemistry for liver-targeted RNA drugs and the template being adapted for other organs.
insights.locator: So researchers attached a sort of address label

insights.claim: Naked siRNA escapes the endosome almost by accident: well under one percent of the molecule leaks out of the endosome into the cell interior, but because siRNA is so potent, that tiny leaked fraction is enough to silence the target gene effectively.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A counterintuitive efficiency point: the entire naked-siRNA drug class works despite a sub-1% delivery efficiency, showing how much headroom for improvement (and thus differentiation among competitors) may still exist in endosomal escape chemistry.
insights.quote: The proportion of siRNA leaking out of endosomes can be well under one percent, but often that is enough because siRNA is so potent – very little of it is actually needed to have its gene-silencing effect.
insights.locator: The answer turned out to be unexpectedly simple

insights.claim: Switching from lipid-nanoparticle patisiran (dosed every three weeks) to GalNAc-conjugated naked siRNA drugs like vutrisiran (dosed every three months, with newer drugs stretching to every six months) cut required dosing frequency roughly four-to-eight-fold for the same disease target.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Dosing frequency is a direct commercial differentiator in chronic-disease drug markets; the naked-siRNA/GalNAc platform materially improves patient convenience and likely adherence versus lipid-nanoparticle predecessors, which matters for market share and pricing power.
insights.quote: is approved to treat the same medical condition, but needs to be dosed only once every three months
insights.locator: The result is a massive difference in how long the drug lasts

insights.claim: GalNAc-conjugated siRNA drugs do not require the immunosuppressant co-therapy that lipid-nanoparticle drugs like patisiran needed, because they avoid triggering the immune reactions associated with lipid nanoparticle carriers.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Removing a co-therapy requirement lowers treatment burden and cost, another commercial edge for the newer naked-siRNA drug class over first-generation lipid nanoparticle formulations.
insights.locator: GalNAc siRNA drugs also have another advantage

themes.theme: The liver franchise and the race to other organs

insights.claim: Multiple siRNA drugs are already FDA-approved for liver-related diseases including hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis, hemophilia, high cholesterol (via inclisiran targeting PCSK9), and acute hepatic porphyria, with more in late-stage trials for hypertension, diabetes, and fatty liver disease.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The liver-targeted siRNA franchise is now a proven, multi-indication commercial category rather than a single-drug proof of concept, giving a template for revenue expansion in adjacent liver diseases.
insights.locator: Multiple siRNA drugs have been approved for treating liver diseases

insights.claim: The liver dominates siRNA's success stories not because siRNA only works there but because the liver's GalNAc receptor pathway made it the easiest organ to target first; the field is now extending the same molecular 'address label' concept to kidneys, lungs, fat tissue, muscle, and brain.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Investors should not treat siRNA as a liver-disease niche technology; the platform's addressable market expands directly with each new organ-targeting chemistry breakthrough.
insights.locator: The reason the liver dominates the story

insights.claim: Competition to extend siRNA delivery beyond the liver is intense, with smaller, aggressive biotech startups such as Manifold Bio and Soufflé Therapeutics positioned to capitalize quickly if an established leader like Alnylam or Arrowhead stumbles.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Names specific emerging competitors worth tracking as potential acquisition targets or share gainers in next-generation organ-targeted RNA delivery.
insights.locator: The competition is intense

themes.theme: The Alzheimer's high-stakes bet: Alnylam vs. Arrowhead

insights.claim: Alnylam and Arrowhead are pursuing rival siRNA strategies against Alzheimer's disease based on the (still-controversial) amyloid hypothesis: Alnylam targets amyloid precursor protein upstream, while Arrowhead targets the downstream tau protein.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Two direct competitors are placing different bets on the same disease mechanism; outcomes will validate or undercut the amyloid-versus-tau debate and reshape which company leads brain-targeted RNA therapeutics.
insights.quote: The most influential theory of Alzheimer’s, though it remains controversial, is that the disease is driven by a misfolded protein, amyloid beta
insights.locator: Among these efforts, the highest-stakes trials

insights.claim: Alnylam and Arrowhead are also taking opposite bets on how to cross the blood-brain barrier: Alnylam uses direct intrathecal spinal injection (effective but uncomfortable and poorly suited to frequent dosing), while Arrowhead is attempting a bolder under-the-skin injection with a proprietary siRNA designed to cross the barrier itself, unproven at this stage.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Arrowhead's approach, if it works, would be a materially more scalable and patient-friendly delivery method than Alnylam's spinal injection, a key technical catalyst to watch in brain-targeted RNA drug trials.
insights.locator: Arrowhead is trying the bolder approach

insights.claim: Even if the amyloid hypothesis is correct and brain delivery succeeds, siRNA may still fail to help Alzheimer's patients because by the time the disease is diagnosed, brain damage is often already extensive enough that clearing amyloid plaques has little effect on halting progression.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A key risk factor for Alzheimer's-focused RNA drug programs: clinical success may hinge on diagnosing and treating far earlier in the disease course than current practice allows, independent of whether the drug delivery technology itself works.
insights.locator: Famously, by the time Alzheimer’s disease is diagnosed

insights.claim: The author's central forward-looking claim is that extending siRNA delivery beyond the liver to other organs is a matter of when, not if, given that the underlying technical approach (molecular targeting labels) has already proven to work.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A high-conviction long-horizon call that the current wave of organ-targeted siRNA trials (kidney, lung, fat, muscle, brain) will eventually succeed, implying sustained multi-year investment opportunity across the RNA therapeutics sector rather than a one-off liver niche.
insights.quote: siRNA delivery beyond the liver is a matter of when, not if.
insights.locator: Yet the broader point still stands

themes.theme: Programmable medicine as an investable platform thesis

insights.claim: siRNA belongs to a broader category the author calls 'programmable medicines': once the delivery chemistry into a specific organ is solved, treating a new disease of that organ requires only specifying a new RNA or DNA sequence, not redesigning the underlying chemistry.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: This is the core economic thesis for RNA-based biotech: R&D cost and timeline per new indication drop sharply once a delivery platform is validated, implying much faster and cheaper pipeline expansion than traditional small-molecule drug development.
insights.quote: Once medicinal chemists have worked out how to get a programmable medicine into a particular organ, all that’s required to treat a new disease of that organ is to specify a new RNA or DNA sequence while holding the chemistry constant.
insights.locator: siRNA falls into the category of therapies

insights.claim: Vutrisiran (for transthyretin amyloidosis) and inclisiran (targeting PCSK9 for cholesterol) work on the exact same chemistry and delivery platform despite treating entirely different diseases, directly demonstrating the sequence-swap economics of programmable medicine.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Concrete proof point that platform reuse across indications is already happening commercially, not just theoretical, supporting rapid pipeline scaling assumptions for GalNAc-siRNA developers.
insights.locator: So vutrisiran, the siRNA treatment for hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis

insights.claim: Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), a separate programmable medicine platform delivered similarly to siRNA, have already shown promising phase two clinical trial results for a tau-targeting Alzheimer's treatment.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A competing RNA-adjacent modality (ASOs) is advancing on the same tau target that Arrowhead's siRNA program is pursuing, adding a third horse to the Alzheimer's programmable-medicine race worth tracking alongside Alnylam and Arrowhead.
insights.locator: One such ASO, targeting the tau protein

insights.claim: CRISPR-based gene editing differs fundamentally from siRNA by permanently altering DNA rather than temporarily silencing gene expression, placing it at the more durable but higher-risk end of the programmable medicine spectrum.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Positions CRISPR and siRNA as complementary rather than competing platforms — CRISPR for permanent correction, siRNA for reversible, dose-titratable suppression — relevant for portfolio diversification across gene-therapy risk profiles.
insights.locator: CRISPR-based gene editing can permanently fix genes

insights.claim: The author predicts that as each organ's delivery problem is solved one by one across the programmable medicine platforms (siRNA, ASOs, mRNA, CRISPR), there will be an 'explosion' of safe, convenient treatments for diseases currently considered untreatable.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A high-conviction, multi-decade secular growth thesis for the entire RNA/gene-therapy therapeutics sector, framed as delivery-chemistry solved organ-by-organ rather than target-by-target, a useful lens for sizing the long-run TAM of biotech platform companies.
insights.quote: As scientists solve each delivery problem, we’ll experience an explosion of safe, convenient treatments against a myriad of diseases that were once considered untreatable.
insights.locator: Each of these forms of programmable medicine
